comment.value:
The paper presents a novel PAC learning framework called the Realizable Statistical Model, which exists between the realizable and fully agnostic settings. The authors introduce an empirical surrogate risk minimization algorithm suitable for this general setting, along with various applications, ranging from binary classification to subset ranking. This paper has received five reviews, with scores varying from weak acceptance to clear acceptance. Overall, all reviewers acknowledge the originality of this learning framework, and most agree on the significance of the learnability results. In summary, this is a valuable contribution to the field of computational learning theory, and I recommend its acceptance.

One of the main weaknesses cited by the reviewers pertains to the lack of clarity regarding certain conditions and results, such as the assumptions about labels and conditional label distributions. However, the authors have made commendable efforts to clarify these points. Therefore, I suggest that they incorporate these improvements in a revised version of the paper.

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for your comments. Please find below our responses to your questions.  

**Q1:**

Line 314. Why is conditional independence not required according to Theorem 5? Can you provide a more explicit clarification?

**Response:**

Theorem 5 requires only that the marginals $P(Y_j = 1 | X = x)$ $(j \in [s])$ of the conditional label distribution be of a specific form (namely, in this case, sigmoid-of-linear form); it does not require that $Y_j$ $(j \in [s])$ be conditionally independent given $X = x$.

**Q2:**

Definition 3 states a lower bound for the surrogate risk difference between a label distribution and some prediction on the dual space. This assumption allows upper bounding L-regret via surrogate regret and effectively hides the dependence on $\tau$. Can you clarify the motivation for this strongly proper composite loss? Given a statistic $\tau$, is there a systematic way to design such a loss $\psi$?

**Response:**

The definition of strongly proper composite surrogate losses for a statistic $\tau$ in Definition 3 ensures the following desirable properties: (a) that the surrogate loss is minimized at (an invertible transformation of) the correct value of the statistic $\tau$; (b) that the minimizer is unique; and moreover (c) that for any "incorrect" vector ${\bf u} \in {\mathcal C}'$ for which $\lambda^{-1} ({\bf u})$ is different from the correct statistic value $\tau({\bf p})$, the surrogate risk at ${\bf u}$ is bounded away from the optimal surrogate risk at $\tau({\bf p})$. Together these properties ensure that minimizing the surrogate loss recovers an accurate estimate of the desired statistic, as well as facilitating a quantitative regret transfer bound. Regarding the design of strongly proper composite surrogate losses: For linear statistics (those that can be expressed as an expectation; this includes all the statistics studied in our paper), one can design a strongly proper composite surrogate loss using Bregman divergences associated with any convex function (the logistic style surrogate losses used in our paper are a special case of this construction); a related study for example can be found in the reference below [AF12] (also cited as ref. [1] in our paper). For nonlinear statistics, the construction is typically done case by case; we are not aware of a general recipe.

[AF12] Jacob D. Abernethy, Rafael M. Frongillo. A Characterization of Scoring Rules for Linear Properties. Proceedings of the 25th Annual Conference on Learning Theory, PMLR 23:27.1-27.13, 2012.

**Q3:**

What are the lower bound and upper bound of the pseudo-dimensions? A discussion on this helps illustrating bounds in the best and worst cases.

**Response:**

The pseudo-dimension of the class of linear functions in $p$ dimensions is known to be exactly $p$. We used this as an upper bound since we consider a subset of *bounded* linear functions, but it is unlikely that it can be improved.

**Q4:**

Line 73. The dependence on $p$ in the derived bounds makes the results look inferior to existing ones. It comes from component-wise decomposition of the function class according to Lemma 1. If we can further make assumptions on the structure of the function class $\mathcal{F}$, and / or the data-generating distribution, can we improve the dependence on $p$?

**Response:**

The dependence on $p$ comes from the upper bound on the covering numbers in the uniform convergence result (in the proof of Lemma 2) in terms of the pseudo-dimension. Using a function class ${\mathcal F}$ of smaller pseudo-dimension would certainly lead to a smaller sample complexity; however the function class ${\mathcal F}$ needs to be matched to the class ${\mathcal Q}$ being assumed for the statistic $\tau$ of interest associated with the data-generating distribution (and so in that case the class ${\mathcal Q}$ would also need to be of lower complexity). It is also possible that alternative uniform convergence/other analyses could lead to improved sample complexity bounds (indeed, based on a question from another reviewer, this seems likely for the binary classification case and we will add a note on it in the final version of the paper if accepted; for multiclass and more general multivariate settings, such improvements are not yet clear).

**Q5:**

Why is the $d_1$ covering number adopted? What are the benefits? What if $l_p$ norm or general norms are adopted instead?

**Response:**

The $d_1$ covering number is equivalent to the $l_1$ norm covering number (with some scaling). We use the $d_1$ covering number since the surrogate loss functions we study are Lipschitz w.r.t. the $L^1$ metric and this allows us to upper bound the $d_1$ covering numbers of the surrogate loss function class $\psi_{\mathcal F}$ in terms of the $d_1$ covering numbers of the component real-valued projection function classes ${\mathcal F}^j$ (Lemma 1). (Moreover, the $d_1/l_1$ covering numbers are upper bounded by other covering numbers, including $d_2/l_2$ covering numbers and $l_\infty$ norm covering numbers.)

**Q6:**

Can you compare your sample complexity bounds with those in [1-2] on structured prediction problems via convex surrogates?

[1] Nowak-Vila, Alex, Francis Bach, and Alessandro Rudi. "Consistent structured prediction with max-min margin Markov networks." In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 7381-7391. PMLR, 2020. 

[2] Ciliberto, Carlo, Lorenzo Rosasco, and Alessandro Rudi. "A general framework for consistent structured prediction with implicit loss embeddings." Journal of Machine Learning Research 21, no. 98 (2020): 1-67.

**Response:**

Thank you for the references. Below we discuss ref. [2] first and then ref. [1]; we will also include a summary of this discussion in the final version of the paper if accepted.

*Comparison with ref. [2] (Ciliberto et al., 2020): This paper studies a setting where the target loss function $\ell : {\mathcal Y} \times \hat{\mathcal Y} \rightarrow R_+$ (in our notation) can be written as $\ell(y, \hat{y}) = \phi_1(y)^{\top} A \phi_2(\hat{y})$ for some embedding functions $\phi_1 : {\mathcal Y} \rightarrow R^k$, $\phi_2 : \hat{\mathcal Y} \rightarrow R^k$ that embed the label space ${\mathcal Y}$ and prediction space $\hat{\mathcal Y}$ into $R^k$ for some integer $k$ (more generally, the paper allows embedding into a Hilbert space $H$; we focus on Euclidean spaces $R^k$ here for simplicity), and for some matrix $A \in R^{k \times k}$. The paper effectively considers the "conditional mean embedding" statistic $q^{\*}(x) = E[ \phi_1(Y) | X = x ]$, and assumes that this statistic belongs to some class of functions (such as multilinear functions or a vector-valued RKHS); this statistic is then estimated by minimizing a quadratic surrogate loss to produce an estimate $\hat{q}(x)$, and for a new instance $x$, a prediction is then made according to $h^{\*}(x) \in \arg\min_{\hat{y} \in \hat{\mathcal Y}} (\hat{q}(x))^{\top} A \phi_2(\hat{y})$ (the paper also studies other estimation procedures and settings where ${\mathcal Y}$ and $\hat{\mathcal Y}$ may be infinite; we focus here on the above setting as it is most related to ours). This setting can be viewed as a special case of our RSM framework; indeed the quadratic surrogate used in the paper is also a strongly proper composite surrogate for the above statistic. The target loss based sample complexity bounds in the paper are of the form $\tilde{O}(\alpha/\epsilon^4)$, where $\alpha$ captures problem-dependent parameters (comparable to our bounds).

*Comparison with ref. [1] (Nowak-Vila et al., 2020): This paper considers a special case of the setting described for ref. [2] above, where $\hat{\mathcal Y} = {\mathcal Y}$ and the loss $\ell$ is symmetric. For this special case, the paper develops a hinge/support vector type convex surrogate loss called the "max-min" surrogate loss, whose minimization does not aim to estimate the statistic $q^{\*}(x)$ above (it is not a strongly proper composite surrogate loss), but rather aims to find a minimizer of the target loss $\ell$ directly (just as the hinge loss for binary classification does not estimate class probabilities but aims to find a minimizer of the 0-1 loss directly). For this surrogate loss, the paper establishes target loss based sample complexity bounds of the form $\tilde{O}(\alpha/\epsilon^2)$, where again $\alpha$ captures problem-dependent parameters. Similar to the case of binary classification with hinge loss, for problems covered by this setting, the bound here is better than those that can be obtained with strongly proper composite surrogate losses as done in ref. [2] above and in our paper.

**Q7:**

Definition 3, should be $\mathcal{C}' \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d'}$ rather than $\mathcal{C}' \in \mathbb{R}^{d'}$ ?

**Response:**

Yes, thank you for catching this typo! We will fix it.

Thank you for your comments. Please find below our responses to your questions.  

**Q1:**  

(a) My main concern is about the significance of the result, as I think assuming a convex surrogate function can solve the problem is a very strong assumption. In fact, I feel that in the distributional free setting, the model considered by the paper cannot be seen as a natural generalization of learning under RCN/Massart noise.

(b) If my understanding is correct, in Table 1, papers such as [1] do not learn an LTF with RCN by optimizing a single surrogate function, due to the small-margin issue. Furthermore, for learning an LTF with Massart noise, [2] shows that no single convex surrogate function can be used to even weakly learn an LTF, even with a large margin. Thus, the algorithmic framework considered by this paper cannot be used to solve these problems, and I think these works are not comparable to the model proposed in this paper. So, I think Table 1 cannot reflect the generality of the framework proposed by this work.

(c) Furthermore, the assumption that the stochastic label is generated by the "sigmoid-type" distribution looks very strong to me. In a very recent paper [3], multi-class linear classification is shown to be computationally hard under very natural RCN assumptions, which means we cannot hope to find a convex surrogate for the multiclass setting, and the "softmax-of-multilinear" assumption is thus a very strong assumption and cannot compete with usual noise assumptions such as RCN.

(d) I would like the author to comment on this concern, depending on which I might adjust my score.

[1] Avrim Blum, Alan M. Frieze, Ravi Kannan, and Santosh S. Vempala. A polynomial-time algorithm for learning noisy linear threshold functions. Algorithmica, 22(1/2):35–52, 1998.

[2] Ilias Diakonikolas, Themis Gouleakis, and Christos Tzamos. Distribution-independent PAC learning of halfspaces with Massart noise. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32: Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems 2019, pages 4751- 4762, 2019.

[3] I. Diakonikolas, M. Ma, L. Ren, and C. Tzamos. Statistical query hardness of multiclass linear classification with random classification noise. CoRR, abs/2502.11413, 2025

**Response:**

(a) First, please note that we are *not* assuming that a given learning problem can be solved using a convex surrogate loss function. What we are assuming is that the conditional label distribution $P(Y | X = x)$ satisfies a certain property - namely, that some vector valued statistic of this distribution belongs to some class of functions (this is the core assumption in our realizable-statistic models (RSMs)). Under this assumption, it turns out that in *many* (but not all) interesting cases, the resulting learning problem can indeed be solved by minimizing a convex surrogate loss, as described in Theorems 1 and 2 in the paper (the learning problem needs to satisfy the conditions of these theorems in order for this to hold).

Second, regarding RCN/Massart noise: Both these noise models can indeed be viewed as special cases of RSMs; however, the associated learning problems do not satisfy the conditions of Theorems 1 and 2, and therefore our algorithmic results do not apply to these models (indeed, we have not claimed so anywhere). To see that RCN/Massart noise models can be recovered as special cases of RSMs, note the following: 

*RCN: Consider the statistic $\tau^{+1}$ defined in Section 3 (just below line 219) and the class of statistic functions $Q^{\textrm{RCN-linear}} := \\{ q : {\mathcal X} \rightarrow [0,1] \ | \ \exists {\bf w} \in R^p, \eta \in (0, 1/2) \ \textrm{s.t.} \ q(x) = (1 - \eta) \cdot {\bf 1}({\bf w}^{\top} {\bf x} \ge 0) + \eta \cdot {\bf 1}({\bf w}^{\top} {\bf x} < 0) \\}$. Then the RSM learning problem $( L^{0-1}, H_{\textrm{linear}}, {{\mathcal D}}_{( \tau^{+1}, Q^{\textrm{RCN-linear}} )\textrm{-RSM}} )$ captures exactly the problem of learning linear threshold functions with RCN. (However, as noted above, this learning problem does not satisfy the conditions of Theorems 1 and 2, and therefore our algorithmic results do not apply to this problem.) 

*Massart noise: Consider again the statistic $\tau^{+1}$ defined in Section 3 (just below line 219) and the class of statistic functions $Q^{\textrm{Massart-linear}} := \\{ q : {\mathcal X} \rightarrow [0,1] \ | \ \exists {\bf w} \in R^p, \eta \in (0, 1/2) \ \textrm{s.t.} \ q(x) \ge (1 - \eta) \ \textrm{if} \ {\bf w}^{\top} {\bf x} \ge 0 \ \textrm{and} \ q(x) \le \eta \ \textrm{if} \ {\bf w}^{\top} {\bf x} < 0 \\}$. (Again, as noted above, this learning problem does not satisfy the conditions of Theorems 1 and 2, and therefore our algorithmic results do not apply to this problem.)

In particular, it introduces a novel framework that generalizes previously studied intermediate PAC learning models between the realizable and agnostic settings, and demonstrates concrete applications to a broad range of complex learning problems, all in a distribution-independent setting with respect to the domain/instance space.

(i) The reviewer states multiple times that the assumption of the conditional label distribution having a "sigmoid-of-linear/softmax-of-multilinear" form is a "strong" assumption. Thank you for your comments. Please find below our responses to your questions.  
 
**Q1:**  
 
For binary classification, it is noted that the sample complexity for squared estimation error is $\tilde{O}(p/\epsilon^2)$, which is worse than $\tilde{O}(1/\epsilon^2)$ for the specialized GLM-tron algorithm. Could you elaborate on the specific aspects of your general analysis that lead to this looser bound? Do you see a path to tightening these bounds while preserving the framework's generality?
 
**Response:**  
 
Our sample complexity result is based on a uniform convergence analysis where the complexity of the function class is measured via $d_1$ covering numbers (we chose $d_1$ as the loss functions we study are Lipschitz w.r.t. the $L^1$ metric, allowing us to upper bound covering numbers of the loss function class $\psi_F$ in terms of those of the component real-valued function classes $F^j$ in Lemma 1); we have upper bounded the $d_1$ covering numbers using the pseudo-dimension, which contributes the $p$ term. The sample complexity result for the GLM-tron algorithm in [21] (Kakade et al., 2011) is somewhat different: it first makes use of an online learning style analysis to upper bound the empirical (squared) error/regret, and then makes use of a uniform convergence argument to show that this also yields an upper bound on the expected (squared) error/regret. The uniform convergence analysis there is based on Rademacher complexities; in particular, the Rademacher complexity term involved in the analysis is upper bounded using an entropy integral involving $\infty$-norm covering numbers, which in turn are upper bounded by dimension-independent (independent of $p$) covering number bounds. This leads to the $\tilde{O}(1/\epsilon^2)$ sample complexity bound in [21]. If we were to use the same dimension-independent covering number bound directly in our analysis (since the $d_1$ covering numbers we use can be upper bounded by $\infty$-norm covering numbers), we would end up with a $\tilde{O}(1/\epsilon^4)$ sample complexity bound in our setting instead of our current $\tilde{O}(p/\epsilon^2)$ sample complexity bound. In the binary case, we could potentially replace our current uniform convergence analysis with the one based on Rademacher complexities as used in [21], which it turns out would also give a $\tilde{O}(1/\epsilon^2)$ sample complexity bound for our setting (we will make a note on this in the final version of the paper if accepted). However, it is not immediately clear how to extend the Rademacher complexity based analysis to multiclass or more general multivariate settings; it is possible that such extensions could be developed (and this could indeed be an interesting direction to explore in the future), but this is beyond the scope of the current paper.

**Q2:**  

The conclusion states that it is an open question whether the sample and computational complexities can be improved. Beyond developing alternative algorithms, do you believe alternative proof techniques applied to the same surrogate risk minimization approach could yield tighter bounds?

**Response:**  
 
It is certainly possible that alternative proof techniques could yield tighter bounds for the same surrogate risk minimization approach in special cases (for example, please see the discussion in the response to Q1 above for the case of binary classification with GLMs/sigmoid-of-linear class probabilities). We are currently not aware of alternative proof techniques that can yield tighter bounds for the general framework we study. However, we do not claim that our bounds are optimal (indeed, optimality is not yet established even for various previously studied special cases); it is plausible that, even in the general case, there could possibly be alternative proof techniques that may yield improvements in the future.

Thank you for your comments. Please find below our response to your question.  
 
**Q1:**  
 
While this work compares with some binary classification methods in the table, it would be better to elaborate more on this comparison, for example, the assumption needed. 
 
**Response:**  
 
Regarding the entries in Table 1: The assumptions associated with the RSM entries in the table can be found in the corresponding sections of the paper. The assumptions associated with the GLM entry can be found at the end of Section 3 (lines 242-247). Here we elaborate on the remaining three entries (we will also try to add these details in the final version of the paper if accepted):  
 
*Noisy LTF with random classification noise (RCN): This model assumes that there is a weight vector ${\bf w} \in R^p$ and a noise parameter $\eta \in (0, 1/2)$ such that for any instance ${\bf x}$, a deterministic binary label is first generated according to the sign of ${\bf w}^{\top} {\bf x}$, and then with probability $\eta$ the label is flipped to the opposite sign. Equivalently, the model can be viewed as assuming that the conditional label distribution is of the form $P(Y = 1 | X = {\bf x}) = (1 - \eta) \cdot {\bf 1}({\bf w}^{\top} {\bf x} \ge 0) + \eta \cdot {\bf 1}({\bf w}^{\top} {\bf x} < 0)$. 
 
*Noisy LTF with Massart noise: This model assumes that there is a weight vector ${\bf w} \in R^p$ and a "noise upper bound" parameter $\eta \in (0, 1/2)$ such that for any instance ${\bf x}$, a deterministic binary label is first generated according to the sign of ${\bf w}^{\top} {\bf x}$, and then with some (unknown) probability $\eta({\bf x}) \le \eta$ the label is flipped to the opposite sign. Equivalently, the model can be viewed as assuming that the conditional label distribution satisfies $P(Y = 1 | X = {\bf x}) \ge (1 - \eta)$ if ${\bf w}^{\top} {\bf x} \ge 0$ and $P(Y = 1 | X = {\bf x}) \le \eta$ if ${\bf w}^{\top} {\bf x} < 0$. 
 
*Single index model (SIM): The assumption here is of a similar form as that for GLMs, namely that $E[Y | X = {\bf x}] = \theta({\bf w}^{\top} {\bf x})$ for some weight vector ${\bf w}$ and transfer function $\theta: R \rightarrow [0, 1]$; however unlike GLMs, where $\theta$ is assumed to be known, in SIMs, both the weight vector ${\bf w}$ and the transfer function $\theta$ are unknown (it is often assumed that $\theta$ satisfies some condition such as a Lipschitz property).

This paper introduces 
Realizable-Statistic Models (RSMs), a PAC learning framework for complex problems with stochastic labels that bridges the gap between the realizable and agnostic settings. The core idea is to assume that a specific vector-valued statistic of the conditional label distribution belongs to a known function class, rather than the labels themselves. The authors present a general theorem showing that minimizing a convex "strongly proper composite surrogate loss" yields computationally efficient learning algorithms with finite sample complexity bounds for these RSMs. This general result is then used to provide PAC learning guarantees with stochastic labels for a variety of problems, including multiclass classification, multi-label prediction, and subset ranking.

summary.value:
The paper proposes and studies a PAC learning model called the Realizable Statistical Model (RSM), which lies between the realizable and fully agnostic settings. In this model, labels are randomly generated conditional on the covariates, but a statistic of the conditional label distribution is constrained to lie within a specified family. This definition is quite general: the standard realizable and agnostic settings, as well as generalized linear models (which lie in between), can all be expressed as special cases of RSM.

The proposed learning approach involves estimating the target statistic via a convex surrogate loss. Theorem 1 shows that a bound on surrogate regret can be translated into a bound on the excess risk for learning of the RSM. The main learning algorithm is empirical surrogate risk minimization, and Theorem 2 provides PAC learning guarantees for RSM using this approach. To show this result, the authors introduce a new lemma that bounds the $d_1$ covering number of the loss function class. 

The second part of the paper focuses on applications, including:
- Binary classification with sigmoid-transformed linear class probabilities,
- Multiclass classification with softmax of a multilinear function over the input,
- Multilabel prediction using sigmoid of multilinear marginals,
- Subset ranking.

Strengths:

- The paper makes important advances in PAC learning. Settings that fall in between agnostic and realizable setting have been extensively studied in the last decades. 
- The paper provides applications of the general result and includes comparison with prior work for the case of binary classification

Weaknesses:

- The paper is dense with technical and long statements and no room for proofs (or proof overviews) in the main body.

summary.value: This paper proposes and studies a robust learning setting called realizable-statistical models. Roughly speaking, the realizable statistical model assumes that the Bayes optimal hypothesis of a distribution of labeled examples can be uniquely recovered via some vector-based statistics. If the loss of the problem can be characterized by the accuracy of the above vector-based statistics, and there is some convex surrogate function that can be used to do the statistics, then one could run a convex optimization algorithms over the sample to solve the learning problem and thus yield a sample and computationally efficient algorithm.  Within this framework, the paper considers several class of classification problems that satisfies a ``sigmoid-type" condition such as binary classification, multiclass classification and ranking and shows that by considering minimizing convex surrogate loss one can efficiently solve these classification problems. Since previous works mostly consider binary classification or real-valued regression problems, the results of the paper could be seen as a generalization of the previous problems.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strength: 
The framework proposed by this paper is general and can be used for analyzing various types of learning problems such as multiclass classification, subset ranking, which cannot solved by most prior works that focus on solving a single index model. Furthermore, this paper is sound and the proofs of most results can be found in the appendix.

Weakness: 

My first concern about this paper is its significance. In fact, for many learning problems with label noise, the core difficulty is that one cannot find a single convex surrogate that can be used to solve the problem directly, even if statistically the ground-truth hypothesis can be uniquely recovered from the label. This often happens when no assumption is made over the marginal distributions. It seems to me that unless a very strong assumption such as the ``simoid-type" assumption is made, it could be very hard to find a single convex surrogate that fits the framework to solve the problem.(See my questions below for details.)

My second concern is about the writing style of the main body. The notation system used by the paper is a bit complicated, and sometimes I had to go over the paper several times to understand the meaning of each notation. Furthermore, after the introduction, there are very few paragraph breaks, and many long equations are in lines, which makes going through the paper more difficult. The writing style should be optimized to make the paper more readable.

questions.value:
My main concern is about the significance of the result, as I think assuming a convex surrogate function can solve the problem is a very strong assumption. In fact, I feel that in the distributional free setting, the model considered by the paper cannot be seen as a natural generalization of learning under RCN/Massart noise.

If my understanding is correct, in Table 1, papers such as [1] do not learn an LTF with RCN by optimizing a single surrogate function, due to the small-margin issue. Furthermore, for learning an LTF with Massart noise, [2] shows that no single convex surrogate function can be used to even weakly learn an LTF, even with a large margin. Thus, the algorithmic framework considered by this paper cannot be used to solve these problems, and I think these works are not comparable to the model proposed in this paper. So, I think Table 1 cannot reflect the generality of the framework proposed by this work.

Furthermore, the assumption that the stochastic label is generated by the "sigmoid-type" distribution looks very strong to me. summary.value: This paper introduces realizable-statistic models with stochastic labels which include both the realizable and agnostic PAC learning as special cases. It is assumed that some statistic comes from some known function class. It shows that, for some common RSM learning problems, convex surrogate risk minimization with strongly proper composite surrogate loss yields computational efficiency and finite sample complexities.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths**
- The studied setting is general and applicable to more complex intermediate PAC learning problems with stochastic labels. It generalizes GLMs and presents comparable but a more unified result.
- Instantiation of the framework into several common learning problems is helpful for understanding the main result.

**Weaknesses**
- The paper lacks discussion on the insights about what the benefits are for designing practical algorithms in the future inspired by the derived theoretical results.
- The motivations and justifications for some important assumptions are unclear. See my comments below for details.

questions.value:
**Major concerns**
- Line 314. Why is conditional independence not required according to Theorem 5? Can you provide a more explicit clarification?
- Definition 3 states a lower bound for the surrogate risk difference between a label distribution and some prediction on the dual space. This assumption allows upper bounding L-regret via surrogate regret and effectively hides the dependence on $\tau$. Can you clarify the motivation for this strongly proper composite loss? Given a statistic $\tau$, is there a systematic way to design such a loss $\psi$?
- What are the lower bound and upper bound of the pseudo-dimensions? A discussion on this helps illustrating bounds in the best and worst cases.
- Line 73. The dependence on $p$ in the derived bounds makes the results look inferior to existing ones. It comes from component-wise decomposition of the function class according to Lemma 1. If we can further make assumptions on the structure of the function class $\mathcal{F}$, and / or the data-generating distribution, can we improve the dependence on $p$?
- Why is the $d_1$ covering number adopted? What are the benefits? What if $l_p$ norm or general norms are adopted instead?
- Can you compare your sample complexity bounds with those in [1-2] on structured prediction problems via convex surrogates?

**Typos**
- Definition 3, should be $\mathcal{C}' \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d'}$ rather than $\mathcal{C}' \in \mathbb{R}^{d'}$ ?

**References** \
[1] Nowak, Alex, Francis Bach, and Alessandro Rudi. "Consistent structured prediction with max-min margin Markov networks." In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 7381-7391. PMLR, 2020. \
[2] Ciliberto, Carlo, Lorenzo Rosasco, and Alessandro Rudi. "A general framework for consistent structured prediction with implicit loss embeddings." Journal of Machine Learning Research 21, no. 98 (2020): 1-67.

title.value: Efficient PAC Learning for Realizable-Statistic Models via Convex Surrogates

abstract.value:
A central question in the theory of machine learning concerns the identification of classes of data distributions for which one can provide computationally efficient learning algorithms with provable statistical learning guarantees. Indeed, in the context of probably approximately correct (PAC) learning, there has been much interest in exploring intermediate PAC learning models that, unlike the realizable PAC learning setting, allow for some stochasticity in the labels, and unlike the fully agnostic PAC learning setting, also admit computationally efficient learning algorithms with finite sample complexity bounds. Some examples of such models include random classification noise (RCN), probabilistic concepts, Massart noise, and generalized linear models (GLMs); in general, most of this work has focused on binary classification problems. In this paper, we study what we call realizable-statistic models (RSMs), wherein we allow stochastic labels but assume that some vector-valued statistic of the conditional label distribution comes from some known function class. RSMs are a flexible class of models that interpolate between the realizable and fully agnostic settings, and that also recover several previously studied models as special cases. We show that for a broad range of RSM learning problems, where the statistic of interest can be accurately estimated via a convex ‘strongly proper composite’ surrogate loss, minimizing this convex surrogate loss yields a computationally efficient learning algorithm with finite sample complexity bounds. We then apply this result to show that various commonly used (and in some cases, not so commonly used) convex surrogate risk minimization algorithms yield computationally efficient learning algorithms with finite sample complexity bounds for a variety of RSM learning problems including binary classification, multiclass
classification, multi-label prediction, and subset ranking. For the special case of binary classification with sigmoid-of-linear class probabilities (also a special case of GLMs), our results show that minimizing the standard binary logistic loss has a similar sample complexity as the GLM-tron algorithm of Kakade et al. (2011), but is computationally more efficient. In terms of the distribution over
the domain/instance space, our results are all distribution-independent. To our knowledge, these are the first such results for PAC learning with stochastic labels for such a broad range of learning problems.
